significance.root_decision: All three parts of Conjecture 5.2 of Cha et al. hold: for every n >= 9, s*_{n-2}(n) = s*_{n-2}(n-1) + 1; for every n >= 7, s*_{n-1}(n) = s*_{n-1}(n-1) + 1; for every n >= 10, s*_n(n) = s*_n(n-1) + 1, where s*_r(n) is the least positive integer beyond which every sum has at least r different partitions into n positive parts with a common product. Both thresholds are shown to exist in every case. The proof has three parts: an elementary stability lemma (below twice the number of parts every partition contains a one, so removing a one is a bijection), explicit infinite families of partitions with equal products that settle all large n, and a certified exhaustive computation for the remaining 77 identities with n <= 34, in which 105 non-existence claims are reduced by padding with ones to 14 enumerations. Lean states partitions as multisets of positive integers and the threshold as the least positive permanent-tail bound, exactly as the source does.
significance.caveat: Bounded literature search only. The general argument is about one page of elementary combinatorics and the rest is a certified finite computation, so a specialist could call the result elementary (cross-model confidence: not routine 0.65; Lean statement equals the printed conjecture 0.97). The journal text (Int. J. Number Theory, 2019) is unread; the zbMATH review says the conjectures are still stated there. The three starting values 9, 7 and 10 are sharp: each identity fails one step below.
